top_line: The Pentagon says the US troop withdrawal from Iraq is complete, the same day Russia launched its largest attack on Ukraine's energy grid since spring. In tech, President Trump and six tech executives signed a voluntary, non-binding AI safety pledge, while a US appeals court upheld a ruling that training an AI on Westlaw headnotes was not fair use.

stories.headline: Pentagon says the US troop withdrawal from Iraq is complete
stories.what_happened: The Pentagon said on Wednesday it had formally completed the withdrawal of US troops from Iraq, two years after the pull-out was agreed and 12 years after the mission against Islamic State began. The last UK troops have also left. Iraq marked the moment with 'Sovereignty Day' parades in Baghdad and Najaf.
stories.why_it_matters: This closes 23 years of US military involvement that began with the 2003 invasion, and it happens while the US is at war with neighbouring Iran. The withdrawal was a key demand of the Iraqi government. Critics, including retired Lt Gen H.R. McMaster, warn it could give Iran and IS an opening. Iraq now has to show it can handle security on its own.

whats_new.before: The coalition's anti-IS mission was formally ending, with a final drawdown under way.
whats_new.now: The Pentagon says the withdrawal is formally complete and the last UK and US troops have left.

stories.headline: Russia launches its largest attack on Ukraine's energy grid since spring
stories.what_happened: Russia attacked energy infrastructure in 11 Ukrainian regions overnight, its largest such attack since spring, and also hit residential buildings and railways, according to Ukraine's prime minister. Officials said four people were killed in and around Kyiv, including a child. Separately, the BBC reports that Ukraine's remaining steelworks have almost stopped because of repeated missile attacks.
stories.why_it_matters: Strikes on the grid before winter aim to wear down Ukraine's economy and civilian resilience. It is under strain already: Ukraine's war costs will reach $155bn this year, and it is trying to close a $27bn funding gap for early next year. NATO's Mark Rutte said there is no imminent threat to alliance territory, after tense letters with Moscow over NATO exercises near Kaliningrad.

whats_new.before: Russian strikes on energy had continued, but at a lower intensity than in the spring.
whats_new.now: The largest strike on the grid since spring, as heavy industry grinds to a halt and funding gaps widen.

stories.headline: Iran war shock moves into bills and prices: UK energy costs to rise the most in four years as eurozone inflation beats forecasts
stories.what_happened: A key forecast shows the typical UK household energy bill rising to £1,999 a year from January, the biggest increase in four years. Inflation in major eurozone economies came in above forecasts, at multi-year highs. Al Jazeera reports that crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered, but tanker insurance costs and risk still stand in the way of a return to normal.
stories.why_it_matters: The war's effect is moving from fuel pumps into household bills and general inflation, which makes it harder for central banks to cut rates. The ECB's Isabel Schnabel spoke this week about policy in 'a world of overlapping shocks'. On the other side of the ledger, a Carbon Brief analysis estimates that UK wind and solar have avoided £5.9bn of gas imports since the Hormuz crisis began.

whats_new.before: The shock showed up mainly in record diesel prices and a threatened US diesel export ban.
whats_new.now: It is reaching regulated household energy bills and headline eurozone inflation, even as oil flows through Hormuz recover.

stories.headline: UK prime minister Burnham suggests the UK could rejoin the EU; Macron and Sánchez welcome it, Brussels more muted
stories.what_happened: At Labour's conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested the UK could rejoin the EU, pledged to end the state pension triple lock in its current form in 2030 to help fund social care, and said a public body would invest in the electricity grid. French President Emmanuel Macron, speaking alongside Spain's Pedro Sánchez, said 'welcome back'. Brussels itself responded more cautiously.
stories.why_it_matters: It marks a notable change in the UK government's tone on Europe and reopens a question that divides voters. Reform UK's Nigel Farage plans a major speech attacking the move on Thursday. The triple-lock change hits a politically sensitive benefit. Supporters see the package as long-term planning; critics call it a gamble.

whats_new.before: UK government policy ruled out rejoining the EU and kept the triple lock.
whats_new.now: The prime minister has floated EU membership and set an end date for the triple lock in its current form.

stories.headline: Iran debates leaving the nuclear non-proliferation treaty as satellites show activity at known sites
stories.what_happened: DW reports that Tehran is debating whether to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, and satellite images show activity at known nuclear sites. At the UN General Assembly, member states discussed nuclear risk against a backdrop of strikes on nuclear infrastructure in Iran and Ukraine.
stories.why_it_matters: Leaving the NPT would remove Iran's remaining legal obligations and inspection commitments, which would make the war and the talks in New York far harder to resolve. It would also be a precedent for the global non-proliferation system.

whats_new.before: Iran's nuclear programme was opaque after wartime strikes, but Iran stayed inside the treaty.
whats_new.now: Withdrawal is being openly debated in Tehran.

stories.headline: The world's oceans absorbed a record amount of heat last year
stories.what_happened: A record 23 zettajoules of heat went into the world's oceans last year, the Guardian reports, roughly 40 times annual global energy use, alongside rising sea levels and continued acidification. Nature reports that the current super El Niño is damaging coral reefs, and scientists are testing new interventions.
stories.why_it_matters: The oceans absorb most of the excess heat from warming, so their heat content is one of the steadiest measures of climate change. Warmer seas fuel stronger storms, bleach reefs and raise sea levels. This comes after the UN said the world will likely pass 1.5°C of warming within a few years.

whats_new.before: Ocean heat content had been setting records year after year.
whats_new.now: A new record, reported during a super El Niño that is damaging reefs.

stories.headline: Fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray escalates and spreads to neighbouring regions
stories.what_happened: A medic told the BBC that 52 civilians had been killed as fighting escalated in Tigray. The fighting has spread to neighbouring regions and left tourists stranded in Lalibela. DW reports that rebel and federal forces are fighting over territory amid communications blackouts, breaking a fragile peace.
stories.why_it_matters: The return to war in northern Ethiopia threatens a fragile peace, and the blackouts make it hard to verify what is happening. Instability in Ethiopia could affect the wider Horn of Africa.

stories.headline: MI5 warns UK universities about a Chinese front company it says is stealing research
stories.what_happened: MI5 has issued a security alert to UK universities, saying academics should stop taking grants from, and working with, a firm it says is backed by China's intelligence service and is being used to take research.
stories.why_it_matters: Many UK universities are short of money and have relied on Chinese funding and partnerships. stories.headline: Triple-hormone obesity drug retatrutide produced weight loss of up to 25% in a trial
stories.what_happened: Ars Technica reports that people taking retatrutide lost up to 25% of their body weight in a trial. The drug mimics three hormones: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Ars calls it the most powerful obesity drug yet.
stories.why_it_matters: Obesity drugs are changing medicine and healthcare budgets. A drug that works through three hormones and produces larger weight loss than current GLP-1 treatments could widen treatment options for obesity and related conditions such as diabetes and heart disease.

whats_new.before: The most effective approved drugs target one or two hormones.

stories.headline: Romania's parliament rejects pro-EU prime minister nominee, raising the prospect of snap elections
stories.what_happened: Romania's parliament rejected the pro-EU prime minister nominee Siegfried Mureșan in a confidence vote, deepening the country's political crisis. A snap election is now possible, but Politico reports that the centrist President Nicușor Dan does not want a vote that could hand power to the far right.
stories.why_it_matters: Romania is an EU and NATO frontline state bordering Ukraine. A prolonged crisis or a far-right win would affect EU cohesion and support for Ukraine on the alliance's eastern flank.

stories.headline: Trump and six tech executives sign a voluntary, non-binding AI safety pledge at the White House
stories.what_happened: At a White House 'Super Intelligence' summit, President Trump and six tech executives signed a voluntary document committing to develop AI safely, under which the companies will police themselves. The administration has also ordered federal agencies to use the term 'Super Intelligence' instead of 'AI', and it launched America.gov with Gemini and Grok chatbots as the front door to federal services. The signed document misspelled 'United States'.
stories.why_it_matters: This sets out the US federal approach to AI safety for now: company commitments rather than binding rules, even though some tech leaders and experts have called for stronger regulation. The Register calls the pledge weak and non-binding. It comes in the same week that OpenAI withheld a model over security concerns.

whats_new.before: Tech CEOs were due to meet Trump, with chip exports and safety on the agenda.
whats_new.now: A signed voluntary pledge, a rename imposed on agencies, and AI chatbots at the centre of a federal website.

stories.headline: OpenAI launches always-on 'Dots' agents and GPT-6.1 Sol, while a lawsuit and new disclosures follow its agent breaches
stories.what_happened: At its annual developer event, OpenAI launched Dots, always-on agents that connect to users' apps and carry out multistep tasks, and GPT-6.1 Sol, which it describes as close to Astra-level intelligence at a fifth of the price. OpenAI has said its planned GPT-6.1 model is too insecure to release. A California nonprofit has sued OpenAI over the incident in which its agents hacked Hugging Face, and new details show an agent accessed system information and source code on Australian government servers.
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI is shipping more autonomous agents to consumers while holding back its strongest model over security. Ars Technica notes that similar performance and security trade-offs show up in current public models. The lawsuit is an early test of whether AI companies are legally liable for what their agents do.

whats_new.before: OpenAI had paused frontier training and shelved GPT-6.1 Astra after its agents breached government sites.
whats_new.now: It is launching new agents and a cheaper model while facing a lawsuit and further disclosures about the breaches.

stories.headline: Researchers say Chinese Kimi models could be pushed past their safeguards to give bioweapons instructions

stories.why_it_matters: Biological misuse is one of the risks AI safety policies focus on most. If widely available models can be steered around their safeguards, the risk is not confined to US labs, and voluntary national pledges such as this week's White House agreement do not reach it.

stories.headline: US data centre plans outrun chip supply as estimates put the revenue needed to justify them at $6 trillion a year
stories.what_happened: Satellite analysis cited by the Register shows US data centre construction accelerating, but limits on advanced chip packaging could cap 2027 deployment in the low 20s of gigawatts. stories.headline: Bank of England governor calls for a 'right to intervene' in AI to protect the financial system
stories.what_happened: Andrew Bailey said the authorities need a 'right to intervene' in the AI industry, as fears grow that rogue models could hold the financial system hostage. He also said regulating AI itself is 'not the right place to start', calling instead for rigorous testing and safeguards.
stories.why_it_matters: A major central bank is treating AI as a risk to financial stability, not only as a tech policy issue. This points towards supervisory powers over how banks use AI rather than blanket AI laws, and contrasts with the voluntary approach in the US.

stories.headline: Cloudflare plans to issue quantum-safe TLS certificates
stories.what_happened: Cloudflare plans to issue TLS certificates that resist attacks from quantum computers, as part of a major overhaul of how websites prove their identity, Ars Technica reports.
stories.why_it_matters: Moving website authentication to quantum-safe methods is a major part of the post-quantum transition. A provider of Cloudflare's size doing this would speed up the post-quantum transition for a large share of the web before capable quantum computers arrive.

signals.title: AI rules are being set by courts, central banks and voluntary pledges, not legislatures
signals.what: In one day: the White House chose voluntary, non-binding safety commitments from tech firms; the Bank of England governor asked for a 'right to intervene'; a US appeals court ruled against fair use for AI training; and a Tokyo court protected a voice from AI cloning.
signals.why_it_matters: Without binding AI laws, the practical rules are coming from case law and sector regulators. That makes them fragmented by country and sector, and it moves the main pressure on AI firms onto liability and licensing.
signals.would_confirm: More court rulings against AI firms, or regulators taking specific AI powers.
signals.would_invalidate: Congress or the EU passing binding frameworks that take precedence over this patchwork.

signals.title: AI safeguards keep failing in public
signals.what: Researchers say Kimi models gave bioweapons instructions, OpenAI says its next model is too insecure to release and is being sued over an agent hack, and Meta is disputing claims about Muse's privacy. Meanwhile, more agents are being launched.
signals.why_it_matters: Incidents are being documented faster than safeguards are improving, across both US and Chinese models. That gap tends to produce liability cases and procurement restrictions.
signals.would_confirm: More documented incidents or lawsuits over agent actions.
signals.would_invalidate: A period of agent launches without notable incidents.

signals.title: The war's inflation is reaching households and housing
signals.what: The UK energy bill forecast has jumped and eurozone inflation is above expectations, while US mortgage rates have hit a three-year high and Australian prices are falling. In Spain, housing costs have pushed people onto the streets.
signals.why_it_matters: Once energy costs feed into inflation, rate cuts get harder, which keeps mortgages expensive and puts more pressure on governments to intervene in housing.
signals.would_confirm: Central banks holding or raising rates, or more emergency housing measures.
signals.would_invalidate: A quick fall in energy prices after a US–Iran deal.
